Author: @NetNephew-h8q
Content:
In the 17th century, a pumpkin was commonly referred to as a pompion or pumpion. The modern spelling of "pumpkin" gradually evolved from these earlier terms. 
Etymology of the pumpkin's name
The name's progression from Greek to English began centuries before the 17th century: 
Greek: The origin of the word is the Greek pepon, which means "large melon".
French: The French changed pepon to pompon.
English: The English then adapted the French term into pompion or pumpion. 
Usage in the 17th century
Colonial America: English settlers in the American colonies used the term pompion for the plentiful orange squash that became a food staple.
Arrival of "pumpkin": The name "pumpkin" first appeared in print in 1647, and American colonists were likely responsible for transitioning the name from pumpion to its modern form.
General squash names: It was also common for 17th-century botanists and colonists to simply group the new-world squash with more familiar Old-World plants like melons and gourds. Botanist John Parkinson wrote in 1640 of "gourds or millions, or pompions, or whatsoever else you please to call them". #GoogleAI

Author: @VB-bk1lh
Content:
How about pumpkin fritters or pumpkin french fries?
I worked with a woman who grew in the Tennessee hills and she used to take pumpkins that were too small to sell or those that were too misshapen and she would treat them just like any other squash, but as a sweet desert vs a regular squash fritter. They were delicious. 
An old woman in the neighborhood where I grew up, who had come over from Italy not long before, apparently didn't know what to do with some pumpkins someone gave her so she cut them into strips and deep fried them like potato fries. She later made some that were breaded and fried like mozzarella sticks.  As kids we found if we brought her  pumpkins, she'd make them bowls of them and bring them around to the neighbors. We brought her a lot of pumpkins. 
My mother would make pumpkin bread or cake, occasionally pumpkin pie but dad would cook it for breakfast with bacon, dipped in egg and fried in the bacon grease. Often with his homemade cornmeal pancakes that to this day I've never been able to replicate.

Author: @biffwellington6144
Content:
It was a good move for the English language to get rid of that weird S that looks like an "f" without the crossbar. 

As you can see in that old recipe, both versions of "s" were in use at the same time. How would you know when to use one instead of the other? I would've guessed pronunciation would be the key, but look at how "raisins" is written. It uses both versions of S, but they're pronounced the same. Why?

German, at least, still has a purpose for a similar letter that looks a little like a capital B and is called "ess-tset." It's a harder S, and it was created by combining that archaic S with a Z (hence the name, which is essentially SZ).

English, though? Yeah, we're better off just using one version of S for everything.

Author: @theunease5541
Content:
I've made this for 3 years now and I'm gonna make it again for this Thanksgiving. It is AMAZING. Just like you say in the original video, apple and pumpion works great together. Then the herbs and dried fruits add such a unique fun flavor complexities and texture. The three different textures from the apple, fruit and pumpion work great. I love it. I have tried a number of alterations in my different attempts too both for convenience and taste.

I have used an assortment of dried fruits including, craisins, raisins, zante currants and dried cherries.

I think I have used marjoram every time and I think it works great.

I generally substitute the sherry for bourbon, (more convenience because it is the alcohol I have, I don't drink. It comes out good though) and I soak the dried fruits in the bourbon while I prepare everything else.

I have layered the dried fruits on top of the apples rather than mixing them in with the pumpion, because I noticed in my oven sometimes the raisins at the top would burn.

This year I think I'm gonna try something different for the pumpion step. I'm gonna try to fry the pumpion in herb infused brown butter. Then use more of that brown butter, along with some fresh herbs mixed into the pumpion "topping".

Will that work at all? Idk, but that's the fun of food sometimes.
